Practice questions of the kinds the midterm asks, on lectures 1 to 7, with feedback on every option. The midterm's questions are different ones.

Numbers in the scenarios are made up for practice unless a price or an instance size is named. If you need to look up a term, the [relevant vocabulary is below](#part-terms).

## Block 1: lectures 1 to 3

### 1. Who is responsible: AWS or you

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## In which service is **AWS** responsible for each of these? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The hardware: the racks and the power :: Both
    > AWS is responsible for the hardware under both: the racks and the power under an instance and under a function. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- The virtual machine layer the code runs on :: Both
    > AWS is responsible for the virtual machine layer under both. An instance is a virtual machine on AWS's hardware; for a function, AWS starts a small virtual machine to hold its execution environment. Where to look: L2 slide 20; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- Patching the operating system :: Lambda
    > On a function, AWS is responsible for the operating system, as it is for the runtime and the capacity. On an instance, the operating system is your responsibility. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- Patching the language runtime the code uses :: Lambda
    > On a function, you pick a runtime version from AWS's list, and AWS is responsible for patching it. On an instance, you install the runtime, so patching it is your responsibility. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- The code that does the work :: Neither
    > You write the code, both on an instance and on a function. AWS is not responsible for it on either. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- The policy that says what your code may touch :: Neither
    > You write the policy, both on an instance and on a function: a role on an instance, an execution role on a function. AWS enforces the policy on both, but is not responsible for writing it. Where to look: L2 slide 30; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- :: EC2
    > Everything AWS is responsible for on an instance, it is also responsible for on a function. AWS is responsible for the bottom two bands on EC2, and for those two plus three more on Lambda. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
```

### 2. Stop or terminate

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## An EC2 instance was launched with its own volume, left on the default of being deleted when the instance is terminated. A second volume was attached later to hold the data, and that one was set to be kept when the instance is terminated. Each volume is billed for the space it takes while it exists. Which condition does each description below fit? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Both volumes are there, and the per-second compute charge is being paid :: Running instance
    > A running instance bills compute by the second, and both volumes bill for their space: nothing has been switched off. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- Both volumes are there and billing, and no compute charge is being paid :: Stopped instance
    > Stopping ends the compute charge and keeps both volumes, which carry on billing for their space. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The launch volume and everything installed on it are kept for the next start, and the compute bill has stopped :: Stopped instance
    > Stopping ends the compute charge and keeps both volumes, which keep billing for their storage, so the instance keeps its data and software for Monday. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The launch volume is gone, and the volume attached later is billing on its own :: Terminated instance
    > Terminating deleted the launch volume because it was set to be deleted. The attached volume was set to be kept, so it remains after termination and keeps billing for its storage. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The launch volume no longer exists, and neither does what was installed on it :: Terminated instance
    > Terminating deleted the launch volume, which was left on its default of being deleted, along with everything installed on it. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- Somebody is logged in right now, and the compute bill is growing by the second :: Running instance
    > A running instance bills compute by the second, and both volumes bill for their storage, whether or not anyone is using the instance. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- :: Instance never launched
    > Every description here is of an instance that was launched with these volumes and is now running, stopped or terminated. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
```

### 3. Launch settings for a notebook instance

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## You launch one EC2 instance to explore a dataset in a Jupyter notebook. The data is 10 GB in a compressed Parquet file in S3. Which launch setting settles each requirement below? Not all options will be used.

- Python 3.12 and the AWS CLI must already be in place the first time the instance boots: no install commands may run at all, not even at first boot :: Image
    > The image is what the instance starts from: its operating system and the software already on it. A user data script could install Python at first boot, but the requirement rules out running any install commands. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- Loaded into pandas, the file takes about 30 GB of memory, and the whole DataFrame must fit in memory at once :: Instance type
    > The type fixes memory, cores and network. Disk space doesn't help: a DataFrame is held in memory, and the file itself stays in S3. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- AWS lets connections reach the instance only on port 8888, and only from your own IP address :: Security group
    > A security group decides which ports are reachable from which addresses. A security group does not check who you are or decide what the instance may read in S3. Where to look: L2 slides 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The notebook reads the file from S3 without anyone putting access keys in a file on the instance :: Role
    > An EC2 instance can be given a role. Its policy says what the instance may read, so no one has to paste access keys into a file on the instance. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- :: User data script
    > Commands the instance runs at first boot. Here everything needed is either in the image or set by another setting. Where to look: L2 slide 25; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- :: Volume size
    > It sets disk space, not memory, and the file is read from S3, not stored on the disk. Where to look: L2 slide 27; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
```

### 4. A function or an instance

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which fits each piece of work best? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A file of a few MB lands in an S3 bucket a few times an hour and needs a few seconds of work to convert :: Function
    > Short work started by an event, the file's arrival, and idle between arrivals. No compute runs or is paid for between calls. Where to look: L3 slides 5, 13 and 39; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A model fit on a 2 GB table that takes forty minutes, cannot be broken into shorter steps, and runs once a night :: EC2 instance
    > A function call stops after fifteen minutes, and the model fit cannot be split into shorter calls. An instance can run the model fit and then stop, and its memory can hold the table. Where to look: L3 slide 13; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- Someone working in a notebook all afternoon on a 5 GB table, changing code and re-running it :: EC2 instance
    > The session has to stay up between keystrokes, and the data in memory has to survive from one cell to the next. Saving files between calls moves the files, not the session. Where to look: L3 slide 5 and L2 slide 19; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A web endpoint answering a few short requests a minute, at all hours, where a second's delay now and then is fine :: Function
    > Short work started by a request, and idle between requests. No compute runs or is paid for between calls. Where to look: L3 slides 5, 13 and 39; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A daily summary of yesterday's 200 MB that takes two minutes and writes one file :: Function
    > Short work started by a schedule, once a day, and idle between runs. No compute runs or is paid for between calls. Where to look: L3 slides 5, 13 and 39; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- :: Cluster of several nodes
    > Every workload here fits on one instance, in its memory and in its time. Several nodes help only when one instance cannot handle the work. Where to look: L4 slides 9–10; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
```

### 5. What starts the function

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A smart-home company runs several functions. What starts the function in each situation below? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Someone asks the voice assistant "what is the temperature?" and it answers a second later :: Request
    > Someone is waiting for the reply: a request starts the function and gets the answer back. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- A thermostat writes a new reading file to a bucket, and a function checks whether it is outside the safe range :: Event
    > The new file's arrival is the event; a rule sends that event to the function. Nobody waits for the check. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- A new firmware file is uploaded to a bucket, and a function checks its signature :: Event
    > The upload is the event; a rule sends that event to the function. Nobody waits for the result. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- A new recording from a door camera lands in a bucket, and a function blurs the faces in it :: Event
    > The recording's arrival is the event; a rule sends that event to the function. Nobody waits for the result. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- Every night at 03:00 a function deletes test devices' logs older than a week :: Schedule
    > A schedule starts the function at a clock time: 03:00 every night. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- On the first day of each month a function totals each household's energy use :: Schedule
    > A schedule starts the function on a calendar date: the first day of each month. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- :: Deployment
    > Deploying a new version puts the code in place. Deploying does not call the handler; the handler runs only when a request, an event or a schedule starts it. Where to look: L2 slide 36 and L3 slides 5, 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
```

### 6. Why the Parquet read is small

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A weather service keeps five years of hourly station readings in S3 as one Parquet file: 9.6 GB, 22 columns of about the same size, sorted by reading time, in 120 row groups of about the same size. A query asks for the average wind speed per station in the first week of July 2024, which needs that week and 3 of the 22 columns. Run with DuckDB, it reads about 20 MB from S3. Which reading explains 20 MB?

1. [x] Needed columns only, from row groups that can contain the week
    > Both savings at once. One week sits in 1 or 2 of the 120 row groups (each about 80 MB with all columns), and only 3 of 22 columns are read from them: about 11 to 22 MB. The footer's minimum and maximum reading time per row group say which row groups can hold that week. Where to look: L1 slides 13–14 and L4 slide 15; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
1. [ ] Only 3 of the 22 columns are read, but from every row group in the file
    > Skipping columns alone would read 3/22 of 9.6 GB, about 1.3 GB. The row groups outside that week are skipped too, from the footer's minimum and maximum. Where to look: L1 slides 13–14; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
1. [ ] Only the row groups that can hold that week are read, but with all 22 columns
    > Skipping row groups alone would read 1 or 2 row groups with every column, about 80 to 160 MB. Each column's bytes are stored apart, so the 19 unneeded columns are skipped too. Where to look: L1 slide 13 and L4 slide 15; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
1. [ ] Footer stores a copy of the needed rows, so no data pages are read
    > The footer holds metadata: where each column chunk of each row group sits, and their minimum and maximum. The rows themselves are read from the data pages the footer points to. Where to look: L4 slide 15; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
```

### 7. Where the S3 client is made

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A Lambda function, with default settings, has the line `s3 = boto3.client("s3")` as the first line of its handler, then uses the client to write one small file. A hundred calls arrive in a minute, one after another, and one execution environment serves them all. Which statement is true?

1. [x] Client is created on every call
    > Everything inside the handler runs on every call. Code at module level runs once, when the environment starts, and the calls after that reuse what it made. Where to look: L3 slide 16 and L2 slide 36; practise [How many times does each line run?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-how-many-times-does-each-line-run).
1. [ ] Client is created once, because Lambda keeps objects made inside the handler between calls
    > The line is inside the handler, so it runs on every call, and the client it makes is gone when the call returns. Only code at module level runs once when the environment starts, so a client made inside the handler is not kept between calls. Where to look: L3 slide 16; practise [How many times does each line run?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-how-many-times-does-each-line-run).
1. [ ] Client is created once, when the code is deployed
    > Deploying puts the code in place. The code does not run until an environment starts to serve a call. Where to look: L2 slide 36; practise [Cold starts, warm calls and memory](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-cold-starts-warm-calls-and-memory).
1. [ ] Client is created once, when the environment starts, as if the line were at module level
    > The line is inside the handler, so it runs on every call, and the client it makes is gone when the call returns. Only code at module level runs once when the environment starts, so this line does not run as if it were at module level. Where to look: L3 slide 16; practise [How many times does each line run?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-how-many-times-does-each-line-run).
```

### 8. Time shape of the demand

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A university runs several cloud-backed services. Which shape does each part of the demand have? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A cache-rebuild run started by a timer at 01:15 every night :: Scheduled job
    > A clock starts one run at a known time each night. Where to look: L2 slide 22 and L3 slides 37–38; practise [What is the time shape of each workload's demand?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-what-is-the-time-shape-of-each-workloads-demand).
- Accepted meal orders: busiest at lunch and dinner, near zero overnight, with the same pattern every day :: Daily rhythm
    > The rate rises and falls in a pattern that repeats each day. Where to look: L2 slide 22 and L3 slides 37–38; practise [What is the time shape of each workload's demand?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-what-is-the-time-shape-of-each-workloads-demand).
- Receipt-rendering runs: one per accepted meal order, with the same lunch-and-dinner pattern :: Daily rhythm
    > Each order starts one receipt run, so the runs have the same daily pattern as the orders. Where to look: L3 slides 37–38; practise [What is the time shape of each workload's demand?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-what-is-the-time-shape-of-each-workloads-demand).
- Room-sensor heartbeats, around the clock: 900 sensors, one every three minutes each, staggered across the three minutes :: Steady rate
    > The staggered sensors produce about the same number of heartbeats every minute. Where to look: L2 slide 22 and L3 slides 37–38; practise [What is the time shape of each workload's demand?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-what-is-the-time-shape-of-each-workloads-demand).
- App opens after an unexpected emergency alert: 4,000 in two minutes, then back to the usual rate :: Burst
    > Many requests arrive in a short interval and then the rate returns to normal. Where to look: L3 slides 37–38; practise [What is the time shape of each workload's demand?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-what-is-the-time-shape-of-each-workloads-demand).
- A full backup started by a timer at 04:00 every Sunday :: Scheduled job
    > A clock starts the run at a known recurring time. Where to look: L2 slide 22 and L3 slides 37–38; practise [What is the time shape of each workload's demand?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-what-is-the-time-shape-of-each-workloads-demand).
```

## Block 2: lectures 4 to 7

### 9. Function, instance or cluster

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which way of running it fits each piece of work best? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A mobile app asks, a few times a minute, for the nearest open store; each answer takes 200 ms to compute :: Lambda function
    > A short answer to a request, with nothing to keep running between requests. Where to look: L7 slide 4, L3 slide 39 and L2 slide 19; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- Every hour an EventBridge schedule starts a check that a website answers, which takes a second :: Lambda function
    > A short task on a schedule, with nothing to keep running between checks. Where to look: L7 slide 4, L3 slide 39 and L2 slide 19; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A model is trained on a 3 GB table for two hours in one Python process, after which the instance is not needed :: One EC2 instance
    > The training uses one process on one instance that holds the 3 GB table. The training takes longer than a function's maximum duration, and only the instance must be stopped afterwards. Where to look: L3 slide 13 and L2 slide 19; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A FastAPI app on port 8000 loads a 2 GB table when it starts and answers `/summary` requests all day :: One EC2 instance
    > The app uses one process on one instance that holds the 2 GB table. It stays up all day, far longer than a function may run, and holds state. Where to look: L3 slide 13 and L2 slide 19; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A Spark job on 3 TB must run on an EC2 instance type that the team picks itself for every node :: EMR cluster you start and stop
    > An EMR cluster lets the team choose the nodes' EC2 instance type; Glue offers worker types instead. 3 TB is too large for one instance. Where to look: L4 slides 9–10; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
- Ten analysts share Spark notebooks on one cluster all week, with node types the team chose :: EMR cluster you start and stop
    > The team picks the nodes' instance type itself, which an EMR cluster lets it do; the cluster stays up all week for many notebooks. Where to look: L4 slides 9–10; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
- :: AWS Glue job
    > On Glue the workers last for one job and nobody picks instances. Every Spark workload here needs chosen node types or a cluster that stays up all week. Where to look: L7 slides 4 and 9.
```

### 10. What Spark can skip

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A scooter-share company keeps its trips as Parquet in S3, in one folder for each trip date: `trip_date=2025-07-01/`, `trip_date=2025-07-02/`, and so on. Each folder holds one file, sorted by scooter id, with about 10 row groups. Each file's footer records the minimum and maximum of each column in each row group, and Spark can use them. Which data can Spark skip for each condition? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-14' AND scooter_id = 'SC-0417'` :: Whole folders and row groups
    > The date names one folder, so the others are skipped. Inside that day's file, sorted by scooter id, the footers rule out the row groups that cannot hold SC-0417. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE trip_date IN ('2025-07-14', '2025-07-15')` :: Whole folders
    > Two folders match by name, and all the others are skipped. Every row in the two matching folders is needed. Where to look: L4 slides 21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE scooter_id BETWEEN 'SC-0400' AND 'SC-0499'` :: Only row groups inside the files
    > The condition does not name the folder column, so every day's folder is opened. Each file is sorted by scooter id, so the footers rule out the row groups outside that range. Where to look: L4 slides 21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE scooter_id = 'SC-0417' AND battery_end < 10`. Every row group has some trips that ended below 10% battery :: Only row groups inside the files
    > The condition does not name the folder column, so every day's folder is opened. Each file is sorted by scooter id, so the footers rule out the row groups that cannot hold SC-0417; the battery condition rules out nothing. Where to look: L4 slide 20; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-14' AND battery_end < 10`. Every row group has some trips that ended below 10% battery :: Whole folders
    > The date skips the other folders. Inside that day's file the battery condition rules out no row group. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-20' AND scooter_id BETWEEN 'SC-0100' AND 'SC-0199'` :: Whole folders and row groups
    > The date names one folder, so the others are skipped. Inside that day's file, sorted by scooter id, the footers rule out the row groups outside that range. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- :: Neither folders nor row groups
    > Spark skips a folder when the condition names the folder column, and a row group when the footer's minimum and maximum rule it out. A condition on the date or on the scooter id always skips something here. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- :: In S3, the rows that do not match
    > S3 hands back the byte ranges Spark asks for. Spark decides what to skip, from folder names and footers. Where to look: L1 slide 14 and L4 slide 15; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read), [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
```

### 11. What happens when each line runs

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## In a PySpark notebook on an EMR cluster, `recent` is a Spark DataFrame of 2025's ticket sales made from Parquet files in S3, `pd` is pandas, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`. What happens when each line runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `venues_pd = pd.read_parquet("s3://tickets-raw/venues.parquet")` :: pandas does the work in the driver only, with no Spark plan
    > pandas reads the file in the driver's process alone, with no Spark plan and no tasks. Where to look: L5 slides 24–25; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
- `pricey = recent.filter(F.col("price") > 100)` :: Spark adds a step to the plan. No task starts
    > A filter is a transformation: it goes into the plan and waits for an action. Where to look: L5 slide 22 and L6 slide 7; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
- `avg_seats = venues_pd["seats"].mean()` :: pandas does the work in the driver only, with no Spark plan
    > pandas computes the mean in the driver's process alone, with no Spark plan and no tasks. Where to look: L5 slides 24–25; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
- `by_price = recent.orderBy(F.col("price").desc())` :: Spark adds a step to the plan. No task starts
    > A sort is a transformation: it goes into the plan and waits for an action. Where to look: L5 slide 22 and L6 slide 7; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
- `n = recent.count()` :: Tasks start on the executors
    > Counting is an action: the plan runs as tasks on the executors, then one number is sent to the driver. Where to look: L5 slides 22 and 24–25; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
- `recent_pd = recent.toPandas()` :: Tasks start on the executors
    > toPandas is an action: the plan runs as tasks on the executors, then every row is sent to the driver. Where to look: L5 slide 24; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
- :: S3 filters the rows before they come to Spark
    > S3 returns the bytes it is asked for. Filters run in Spark's tasks, or in pandas on the driver. Where to look: L5 slide 22; practise [What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-what-runs-where).
```

### 12. Where each thing is kept

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A PySpark notebook on an EMR cluster reads a month of parcel scans, stored as 30 daily Parquet files, and writes each depot's totals as Parquet. The cluster is terminated at the end of the day. Where is each thing below kept while the notebook runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The 300 depot totals, turned into a pandas DataFrame with toPandas() to draw a chart in the notebook :: In the memory of the driver
    > A pandas DataFrame lives in the driver's process: toPandas() brings the 300 rows there from the executors. Where to look: L5 slides 24–25; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A small list of depot names read with pd.read_csv in the notebook :: In the memory of the driver
    > A pandas DataFrame lives in the driver's process: pd.read_csv is pandas, not Spark, and runs in the driver alone. Where to look: L5 slides 24–25; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- Files an earlier job saved on the cluster's HDFS for a later job on the same cluster :: On the disk of a node
    > HDFS keeps its blocks on the core nodes' disks, which go when the cluster does. Where to look: L5 slides 18 and 33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A temporary file a task creates in its node's local folder and deletes before the task ends :: On the disk of a node
    > A task's scratch file is on the disk of the node that runs the task. The node's disk goes when the cluster is terminated; the task deletes the file earlier, when the task ends. Where to look: L5 slides 18, 24 and 33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A public Parquet dataset that several teams' clusters read :: In an S3 bucket
    > S3 keeps the dataset after any cluster is terminated, while a cluster's disks go with the cluster, so many clusters can share the dataset. Where to look: L5 slides 18, 24 and 33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A results file a teammate opens next week, after this cluster is terminated :: In an S3 bucket
    > S3 keeps the results file after the cluster is terminated, while the cluster's disks go with it, so a teammate can open the file next week. Where to look: L5 slides 31 and 33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- :: In the Glue Data Catalog
    > The catalog keeps table definitions, the metadata, not the rows. None of these is a table definition. Where to look: L7 slide 8.
```

### 13. Fewer slots

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## To save money, a cluster shrinks from 2 core nodes to 1, so from 8 slots to 4. In one scan stage, 12 tasks read rows, and each takes about the same time. A task starts when a slot is free, and nothing else changes. How does the stage's time change?

1. [x] It grows to about one and a half times the old time
    > On 8 slots, 12 tasks run in two waves: 8, then 4. On 4 slots they run in three waves of 4. Where to look: L6 slides 23–24; practise [What sets the time of stage 1?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-can-we-speed-up-stage-1-with-more-cores).
1. [ ] It grows to about twice the old time
    > Half the slots does not mean twice the waves. Count them: two before, three after. Where to look: L6 slide 24; practise [What sets the time of stage 1?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-can-we-speed-up-stage-1-with-more-cores).
1. [ ] It grows to about three times the old time
    > Three waves on 4 slots take about one and a half times as long as two waves on 8 slots. Where to look: L6 slide 23; practise [What sets the time of stage 1?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-can-we-speed-up-stage-1-with-more-cores).
1. [ ] It stays about the same
    > With 4 slots, 4 of the 12 tasks now wait for a free slot, so a third wave is added. Where to look: L6 slide 23; practise [What sets the time of stage 1?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-can-we-speed-up-stage-1-with-more-cores).
```

### 14. Row groups and tasks

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A 230 MB Parquet file holds 6 row groups of about the same size. The cluster grows from 8 slots to 16, and Spark's scan of the file now makes 16 tasks. How many of those tasks read rows?

1. [x] 6
    > Spark cuts the file into about 16 byte ranges, and each row group is read whole by the one range that holds its middle. The 6 middles fall in 6 different ranges, so 6 tasks read rows and 10 read none. Where to look: L6 slides 28–29 and 20.
1. [ ] 16
    > Every task gets a byte range, but a range that holds no row group's middle reads no rows. A row group is never split between tasks and never read twice. Where to look: L6 slide 28.
1. [ ] 12
    > A row group is never split between tasks: the one task whose range holds its middle reads all of it. Each of the 6 row groups is read by one task, not by two. Where to look: L6 slide 28.
1. [ ] 1
    > A file with a single row group gives one task that reads rows. Here the 6 row groups have 6 middles, spread across the file. Where to look: L6 slides 20 and 29.
```

### 15. Nodes for a deadline

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A mapping company must render 1,800 satellite image tiles on an EMR cluster before the morning. The tiles are independent of each other, and each takes 6 minutes on one vCPU. They can be spread over any number of vCPUs with no overhead. The cluster has one primary node, which renders nothing, plus core nodes of type m6a.xlarge, each with 4 vCPUs for rendering. Launch takes 15 minutes before the first tile can start, and everything must finish 3 hours after the cluster starts, launch included. Step 1: how much work is it, in vCPU-hours?

1. [ ] 10,800
    > That is the work in vCPU-minutes. Divided by 60 it is 180 vCPU-hours. Where to look: L4 slide 35; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [x] 180
    > 1,800 tiles × 6 minutes is 10,800 vCPU-minutes, which is 180 vCPU-hours. Where to look: L4 slides 35–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither), [How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-how-many-tasks-can-this-cluster-run-at-once).
1. [ ] 1,800
    > That is the number of tiles. Each one is 6 minutes of one vCPU's work. Where to look: L4 slide 35; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [ ] 45
    > 45 is node-hours: 180 divided by a node's 4 vCPUs. The work itself is 180 vCPU-hours. Where to look: L4 slide 37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).

## Step 2: what is the smallest number of core nodes that finishes in time?

1. [ ] 15
    > 15 nodes ignores the launch: 180 vCPU-hours over the full 3 hours is 60 vCPUs, but only 2 hours 45 minutes are left for rendering. Where to look: L4 slides 36–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [ ] 16
    > Sixteen nodes give 64 vCPUs. 180 vCPU-hours over 64 vCPUs takes about 2 hours 49 minutes: over the 2 hours 45 minutes left once the launch is taken out. Where to look: L4 slides 36–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [x] 17
    > After the 15-minute launch, 2 hours 45 minutes are left. 180 vCPU-hours over 2.75 hours needs about 65.5 vCPUs at once. At 4 vCPUs per node, 65.5 vCPUs need 16.4 nodes, rounded up to 17. Where to look: L4 slides 35–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither), [How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-how-many-tasks-can-this-cluster-run-at-once).
1. [ ] 45
    > 180 vCPU-hours divided by 4 vCPUs per node is a number of node-hours, not of nodes. It still has to be spread over the hours left. Where to look: L4 slide 37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
```

### 17. Why the stage is slow

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After an Exchange by store, a stage runs 200 tasks. The median task takes 0.3 seconds on about 50 thousand rows; one task takes 40 seconds on 9 million rows. What is the most likely cause of the slow stage?

1. [x] One key has many more rows than the others
    > After the Exchange, every row with the same key goes to one task, so one task gets all the rows of a store with far more rows than the others. Where to look: L6 slides 30, 48–49; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
1. [ ] Rows each task holds do not fit in the memory available to that task
    > The tasks share each executor's memory on equal terms. One task with 180 times the median's rows points to how the rows were divided, not to how much memory each task has. Where to look: L6 slide 46; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
1. [ ] Too few readable parts of the input
    > That shows up in a scan stage, as tasks that read no rows. This stage comes after an Exchange. Where to look: L6 slide 28; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
1. [ ] Too many small files and folders
    > Small files slow down listing and the start of a scan. They do not make one task after an Exchange over a hundred times the others. Where to look: L6 slides 47–48; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
```

## A team moves a nightly PySpark job from an AWS Glue job to an EMR cluster on EC2. On EMR, what does the team now choose that it did not choose on Glue?

    > On EMR the team rents nodes and picks their instance types. On Glue the team picks a worker type and a count, not EC2 instances. Where to look: L7 slides 4–5.

### 19. A slow window query

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## An online shop's PySpark job on an EMR cluster computes, for each customer, a running total of their orders in date order: a window query over each customer. The shop has 50,000 customers with about 40 orders each, and one reseller account placed 2 million orders. After the `Exchange` by customer, one task takes 25 seconds and the median task 0.2 seconds. Select every statement that is true.

- [ ] For the running-total window, Spark replaces each input task's reseller rows with one partial total before the `Exchange`
    > False. The window produces a running total for every order, so Spark must keep and move the reseller's individual rows. Partial totals are sufficient for a count or sum per customer, but not for this window. Where to look: L6 slides 35–36; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
- [x] Salted customer files can parallelize the reseller's rows in a later scan
    > True. The salt can place one customer's rows in several files, allowing a later file scan to assign those files to several tasks. The customer-keyed `Exchange` for this window will still bring the reseller's rows back to one task. Where to look: L6 slide 39; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
- [ ] Sorting all orders by date before the window removes the reseller skew after the `Exchange`
    > False. The window partitions by customer. After the `Exchange`, all orders for the reseller still meet in one task, regardless of their earlier date order. Where to look: L6 slide 35; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
- [x] A count per customer uses partial totals before the `Exchange` instead of sending every order
    > True. Each input task first counts its local rows for a customer, so the `Exchange` moves partial counts rather than all 2 million reseller orders. Where to look: L6 slides 35–36; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
- [ ] An `Exchange` by customer spreads the reseller's orders evenly across output tasks
    > False. Partitioning by customer sends rows with the same customer key to the same output task. Spreading the reseller's orders evenly would break the grouping by customer that the window needs. Where to look: L6 slide 35; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
```
